artifacts.search_text: mic-elec-ohmic-model-test core1a ohmic behavior is a tested model, not a permanent label a constant-resistance ohmic model is supported only when one device keeps the same voltage-to-current ratio across operating points while the relevant conditions are held fixed; changing the operating condition can make that model stop fitting. every electrical component has one fixed resistance, so a constant-resistance model always applies. use the measured voltage-current pattern first; keep one constant resistance only when the ratio stays unchanged under the stated fixed conditions.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-graphical-subtraction core1a subtraction as addition of the reversed vector see p - q as p + (-q): reverse q's arrowhead without changing its length, then apply tail-to-head addition. vector subtraction means drawing both vectors from the same origin and connecting their two tips in whichever order looks right. perform the explicit reverse-then-add construction (gs-1 to gs-3); the two-tips shortcut hides the observer order and is easy to reverse by mistake. reversing a vector changes its magnitude. reverse only the direction. keep the arrow length fixed; vector negation changes orientation, not magnitude.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-mag-field-direction core1a one magnetic direction, several page marks magnetic field b is an axial vector: its direction is tied to an oriented rotation convention, and dot/cross marks encode out-of-page and into-page directions rather than particle paths. magnetic field lines begin at a north pole and end at a south pole everywhere. treat field lines as a direction map: they continue in closed loops, including through the magnet.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-mag-flux-orientation core1a through-going field depends on surface orientation magnetic flux measures the component of magnetic field through an oriented area; changing the surface orientation changes flux even when b and area size stay fixed. flux is just magnetic-field strength times area, so orientation does not matter. project the oriented area along the field direction: the dot product selects the component through the surface.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-mag-redirect-not-speed core1a a perpendicular magnetic force redirects without speeding up when the magnetic force is perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity, it can continually turn the velocity arrow without lengthening or shortening it; the magnetic interaction redirects motion without supplying kinetic energy. a magnetic field makes a charged particle speed up simply because a force acts on it. compare the force with the instantaneous velocity: a perpendicular magnetic force turns the motion, while its zero dot product with velocity means it does not add kinetic energy.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-measured-from core1a a number alone does not say where something is "where is it?" has no answer until you say measured from what. position is a relation, not a property of the object. position is a property the object carries with it. say what you measured from, then give the number; the number alone is not the answer.

artifacts.search_text: mic-opt-lens-equation core1a use the signed thin-lens equation only after the ray model fixes the geometry the lens equation is a signed coordinate model for the same paraxial image already constrained by the ray diagram; it is not an isolated formula or a mirror relation with copied signs. the spherical-mirror equation 1/v + 1/u = 1/f can be copied unchanged for a lens. identify the optical model first. for the grade-10 thin lens use 1/v - 1/u = 1/f with one declared cartesian convention.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-opt-lens-magnification core1a lens magnification sign carries image orientation one signed ratio links longitudinal image placement and transverse image orientation: magnitude gives relative size while sign distinguishes erect from inverted. magnification is only a positive size factor, so its sign can be discarded. keep m signed. use |m| for relative size and the sign of m for orientation.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-opt-lens-power core1a lens power is signed inverse focal length in metres power compresses focal-length strength into an inverse-metre quantity, so both the metre conversion and focal-length sign are essential. focal length in centimetres can be inserted directly into p = 1/f to obtain dioptres. convert f to metres first, then take the reciprocal and keep the sign.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-opt-lens-ray-construction core1a a thin lens image must be supported by independent principal rays several principal-ray rules are alternative constraints on one thin-lens ray bundle; any valid pair must locate the same image point. any ray through the optical centre of a thin lens must bend toward the focus. use the thin-lens principal-ray rule: a ray through the optical centre is treated as undeviated in the simple paraxial construction.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-opt-mirror-equation core1a the mirror equation is a signed paraxial model of the ray geometry the equation 1/v + 1/u = 1/f does not replace the ray picture: signed u, v and f must refer to the same mirror geometry and the formula is used only within the paraxial/small-angle model. the mirror formula is an exact law for every ray on any part of a spherical mirror, so ray height and aperture never matter. not necessarily. state the paraxial/small-angle approximation before using the simple mirror equation; wide-aperture disagreement can be a model-limit effect.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-opt-mirror-magnification core1a signed magnification carries image size and orientation mirror magnification is not merely 'times bigger': m = h_i/h_o = -v/u is signed, so |m| gives relative size while the sign records erect versus inverted orientation under the declared convention. magnification is only a positive size factor, so taking |m| loses nothing important. no. preserve the sign: |m| describes relative size while the sign carries orientation under the declared convention.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-opt-normal-reflection core1a measure reflection from the normal, not the surface angles in specular reflection are measured from the surface normal, and the reflected ray leaves with the same angle to that normal as the incident ray. the angle of incidence is measured from the mirror surface. draw the normal first; incidence and reflection angles are defined from that line, not from the surface.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-opt-real-virtual-image core1a real and virtual describe how light paths meet an image location is determined by where reflected rays actually meet or where their backward extensions appear to meet; virtual describes ray geometry, not whether a camera can record it. a virtual image is not a usable image and therefore cannot be photographed. separate image geometry from recording: the mirror sends diverging rays that a camera lens can collect and refocus.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-opt-refraction-normal core1a refraction begins with the normal and the two media the bend is a normal-referenced consequence of entering a medium with a different light speed/index; a parallel-sided slab applies the rule at two boundaries. the angle of refraction is measured from the glass surface, so a ray along the normal has a 90-degree incidence angle. draw the normal first. a ray along it has zero incidence angle and continues without a directional bend even though its speed changes.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-opt-refractive-index-snell core1a refractive index connects speed change to snell geometry the same material property that reduces light speed determines the normal-referenced angle relation across a boundary. a medium with a larger refractive index lets light travel faster. use n = c/v. with the same c, increasing n requires a smaller v.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-opt-sign-convention core1a optical signs come from declared directions the cartesian sign convention turns a mirror diagram into signed distances and heights; the signs come from declared directions, not from memorized object/image labels. object distance is always negative and image distance is always positive. apply the coordinate convention from the pole every time; signs follow measurement direction and height orientation.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-opt-spherical-ray-construction core1a principal rays are consistent shortcuts to one spherical-mirror image a small set of principal-ray rules are not independent tricks: any valid pair for the same object point and spherical mirror must locate the same image point within the model. any two memorized principal-ray sketches can be combined even if they predict different image points. no. recheck the mirror type, focus/centre side and before/after ray directions until all valid rays agree on one physical or backward-extension intersection.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-osc-energy-exchange core1a energy trades twice during one displacement cycle in an ideal oscillator, energy shifts between motion and displacement storage while the total stays fixed; the energy state is the same at equal-magnitude displacements on opposite sides, so the kinetic-potential pattern repeats twice during one full displacement cycle. potential energy becomes negative whenever displacement is on the negative side of equilibrium. treat the side of equilibrium and the stored-energy amount separately: opposite equal-magnitude displacements have the same potential-energy state.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-osc-stable-equilibrium core1a repetition is not enough: look for a stable equilibrium an oscillation is organized around a stable equilibrium: when displaced, the system has a tendency that points back toward that equilibrium. any motion that repeats is automatically simple harmonic motion. separate periodicity from the restoring condition; repetition by itself does not identify simple harmonic motion.

artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-fluid-r2 core1a buoyant force follows displaced fluid buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid, so submerged volume and fluid density—not the object's mass by itself—set the buoyant force. objects with equal mass experience equal buoyant force in the same fluid. compare displaced volumes: buoyant force follows the weight of displaced fluid, not the object's mass label.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-fluid-r3 core1a steady incompressible flow speeds up in a narrower section for steady incompressible flow through one tube, the volume-flow rate is conserved, so smaller cross-sectional area requires larger flow speed. water must slow down in a narrower pipe because there is less space available. conserve volume flow rate: the same volume per time must pass every section, so area and average speed vary inversely.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-fluid-r4 core1a pressure, speed and height trade along an ideal-flow path along a streamline in steady ideal flow, pressure, kinetic, and gravitational energy-per-volume contributions trade; a speed increase alone does not determine the pressure change unless the other contributions are controlled. wherever fluid speed is higher, static pressure must be lower, regardless of height or losses. use all bernoulli terms between points on the same streamline and state the ideal-flow assumptions before drawing a pressure conclusion.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-grav-free-fall-g core1a local gravitational acceleration: force per unit mass and free-fall mass independence at one field point in the newtonian test-mass model, local g is gravitational force per unit test mass. combining f_grav = g m m/r^2 with f_net = m a cancels the test mass, giving local acceleration proportional to m/r^2 rather than to the falling object's mass. a heavier object has a larger gravitational force, so it must have a larger ideal free-fall acceleration. use the same mass in both gravity and f = m a. force and inertia both scale with test mass, so the mass factor cancels from acceleration. gravitational force and local g are the same physical quantity. local g is force per unit mass. different masses can feel different forces at the same location while sharing the same local g. g is universally 9.8 m/s^2 everywhere. no. the familiar near-earth value is a local approximation; outside the source, the newtonian model gives local g proportional to m/r^2.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-grav-inverse-square core1a universal gravitation: model scope, centre distance and inverse-square scaling within the newtonian point-mass model, or outside a spherically symmetric source where the external reduction is valid, f = g m1 m2/r^2 uses centre-to-centre separation; masses enter linearly, distance through the inverse square, and direction remains toward the attracting source. doubling the separation halves the gravitational force. apply the square to the distance factor: 2r contributes 1/2^2 = 1/4. for spherical bodies, r in the simple inverse-square relation is the gap between the surfaces. use the centre-to-centre separation. the external spherical reduction treats the source mass as if concentrated at its centre. the computed gravitational-force direction should be chosen from the object's motion direction. no. keep the force attractive along the source-receiver line; motion direction is a separate vector.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-grav-mass-weight core1a mass stays with the object; weight is its local gravitational force for the same object, mass is kept distinct from local gravitational acceleration, while weight is the gravitational force w = m g and therefore changes if local g changes. mass and weight are the same quantity, so a smaller weight reading means the object's mass decreased. keep the object's mass fixed. weight is the local gravitational force w = m g, so changing g changes weight without changing mass. because local g is often written near 9.8, weight is effectively a fixed property of the object everywhere. no. weight follows the local g through w = m g; the same object's mass is the quantity held fixed.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-grav-r1 core1a gravity is a persistent mutual attraction fixed by source-receiver geometry in the newtonian model, the two bodies exert equal-and-opposite attractive forces on distinct receivers along the line joining their centres; support or motion state does not switch the interaction on or redirect it. the larger body pulls on the smaller body, but the smaller body does not exert an equal gravitational interaction back. draw the two forces as an interaction pair on different receivers: force on apple toward earth and force on earth toward apple. gravity acts only while an object is falling; support or upward motion turns gravity off. keep the gravity arrow present whenever the mass-source interaction and newtonian model apply; support or velocity changes other forces/motion, not the existence of gravity. the gravitational-force direction follows the object's velocity or always points down the page. use the source-receiver line. the force points toward the attracting source regardless of the object's instantaneous velocity or page orientation.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-grav-r4 core1a gravitational binding uses a chosen zero of potential energy gravitational potential energy is negative when zero is chosen at infinite separation, and changes in that energy trade with kinetic energy in orbital and escape problems. negative gravitational potential energy means the object has negative total energy in every gravitational motion. keep potential, kinetic, and total energy separate; the sign of one term does not determine the sign of each other term.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-grav-r5 core1a central gravity conserves orbital angular momentum about the centre a central gravitational force has zero torque about the source centre, so orbital angular momentum is conserved; its axial-vector direction is perpendicular to the orbital plane. angular momentum points along the direction the satellite is moving around the orbit. use the cross-product orientation: position and momentum lie in the orbital plane; angular momentum is axial and normal to that plane.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-kin-2d-constant-acceleration core1a apply constant-acceleration kinematics component by component the one-dimensional constant-acceleration equations can be applied to each perpendicular component independently when a_x and a_y are each constant over the same interval. the magnitude of acceleration should be inserted unchanged into both x and y equations. no. use a_x=10 only in the x equation and a_y=4 only in the y equation; the magnitude is not either component. if one acceleration component is constant, the constant-acceleration equations are automatically valid on both axes. no. model validity is checked per axis. a constant a_x does not make a_y constant. a time found from the x equation may be replaced by a different convenient time in the y equation. use t=3 s. both components describe the same event and therefore share one clock.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-kin-2d-independent-components core1a split one plane-motion event into independent x/y components with one clock perpendicular components may be solved separately because each axis equation contains only that axis's quantities, but they still describe one object at one physical time. independent x and y motions may use different elapsed times. no. independence separates the axis equations; it does not give the same object two clocks. the x-motion and y-motion are two different objects that can be paired arbitrarily later. no. a plane state is a simultaneous pair. recombine x(t) and y(t) only at the same t in the same frame.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-kin-average-rates core1a average speed and average velocity come from different totals average speed divides total path length by total time, while average velocity divides signed displacement by that same time; neither is obtained by averaging listed speeds unless the weighting justifies it. average speed is always the arithmetic mean of the speeds listed for the trip. build total distance and total time first. only equal time weighting permits an unweighted arithmetic mean of speeds.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-kin-circular-dynamics-role core1a circular dynamics: centripetal is a net-force role, not a new force the inward acceleration requirement v^2/r fixes only the net radial component m v^2/r; tension, friction, gravity, normal force, or combinations may supply that resultant, so 'centripetal force' must not be added as another interaction. tension plus an additional centripetal force both point inward. draw the string tension only; 'centripetal' names the role of the net inward component. a cut string makes the object fly radially outward. keep the instantaneous tangent velocity; removing tension removes inward acceleration, not the tangent velocity. static friction on a flat curve always equals mu_s n. compute m v^2/r first and compare that demand with the static bound.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-kin-constant-acceleration core1a derive the constant-acceleration equations from one velocity-time graph one straight velocity-time segment carries all three grade 9 kinematic equations: its slope gives v = u + at, its rectangle-plus-triangle area gives s = ut + 0.5at^2, and combining trapezoid area with the slope relation eliminates time to give v^2 = u^2 + 2as. the constant-acceleration equations are independent formulas to memorize rather than consequences of one straight velocity-time graph. return to the graph: slope must be constant. derive the equations from that slope and the graph area before using them. gravitational acceleration is -g while the object rises and +g after it starts falling. no. keep the chosen axis fixed. with +up, gravity remains a=-g throughout the bounded flight; only velocity changes sign at the turning point.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-kin-distance-displacement core1a path travelled is not start-to-finish change distance counts the whole route travelled, while displacement records only the directed change from start to finish; a return to the start leaves zero displacement after a nonzero journey. distance travelled and displacement are always the same number. count every part of the route for distance; compare only the start and finish for displacement, keeping the declared direction.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-kin-motion-graphs core1a motion graphs turn coordinate change into rate on a position-time graph, segment slope is average velocity over that interval; on a velocity-time graph, segment slope is average acceleration. graph height and graph slope answer different physical questions. a higher point on a motion graph always means the object is moving faster. read slope, not page height, for rate: a horizontal position-time segment has zero average velocity.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-kin-projectile-model core1a select the gravity-only projectile model before using projectile consequences after release in the ideal near-earth model, projectile motion is not a new set of laws: it is the same component kinematics with a_x=0 and a_y=-g (for +y upward). a projectile needs a horizontal force to keep moving horizontally. yes. zero horizontal acceleration means horizontal velocity stays constant, not that it becomes zero. a horizontal launch has no vertical velocity throughout the flight. no. u_y=0 only at release; a_y=-g makes v_y=-gt afterward. at the highest point the whole velocity and the acceleration are both zero. only v_y is zero at that instant. v_x remains u_x and a_y remains -g. same-height flight formulas may be used whenever the question is about a projectile range or flight time. no. same-height shortcuts require delta y=0 between launch and landing. for unequal heights, solve the vertical position condition. at two points of the same height on an ideal trajectory, the velocity vectors are identical. v_x is the same, while v_y has equal magnitude and opposite sign; the speed matches but the velocity vector does not. horizontal speed determines how long a horizontally launched object takes to fall. no. the vertical position equation determines the fall time; horizontal speed changes the range, not the fall time.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-kin-uniform-circular-motion core1a uniform circular motion keeps speed while velocity turns an object moving around a circle at constant speed is still accelerating because velocity direction changes continuously; velocity is tangent, acceleration points inward, and the constant speed for one revolution is circumference divided by period: v = 2 pi r / t. constant speed means zero acceleration. compare the tangent directions at different points: the direction changes, so velocity changes and acceleration is nonzero.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-kin-zero-v-nonzero-a core1a zero velocity at an instant does not mean zero acceleration velocity and acceleration answer different questions: velocity can be zero at one instant while a nonzero acceleration determines the change through that instant. if velocity is zero at an instant, acceleration must also be zero at that instant. compare moments immediately before and after the top; the velocity changes from upward to downward, so acceleration remains nonzero through the zero-velocity instant.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-machine-compare core1a levers, pulleys and inclined planes realize different force-distance tradeoffs a lever, pulley or inclined plane should be analysed by its input/output force, direction and distance tradeoff rather than by a memorized claim that every simple machine reduces force. every pulley, lever or inclined plane must reduce the effort force. it can reverse the direction of the required effort. identify the actual setup before claiming force advantage.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-machine-ma core1a mechanical advantage is a same-state load-to-effort force ratio mechanical advantage is the dimensionless same-state force ratio ma = f_load/f_effort; a practical demonstration must measure both forces for one steady setup before forming the ratio, and the result says nothing by itself about efficiency. mechanical advantage is the same as efficiency. yes. ma compares forces only; a machine can be useful by changing force direction even with ma = 1. a load reading from one lever setting can be divided by an effort reading from a different setting to calculate mechanical advantage. no. measure load and effort for the same steady setting, then calculate ma for that state. compare separate same-state ratios across controlled settings.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-machine-tradeoff core1a a machine trades force or direction for distance; it does not create work a simple machine can reduce effort force or change its direction by requiring a different input distance; in the ideal model input work equals useful output work. if a machine gives a larger output force than the effort force, it creates energy. track both force and distance. in an ideal machine, a force advantage requires a compensating distance tradeoff.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-nlm-connected-common-accel core1a connected bodies and a justified common acceleration bodies share an acceleration component only when a physical constraint keeps their relative separation fixed along that coordinate; the shared acceleration can link separate newton-ii equations, while internal partner forces cancel only if the bodies are deliberately treated as one system. any two touching or connected bodies automatically have the same acceleration. name the active constraint first. equal acceleration is justified only while the relative-separation condition remains enforced. the contact force between two bodies can be cancelled from each individual fbd because it is an internal force of the pair. yes. keep it in a's equation. it cancels only after a and b are deliberately combined into one system equation. bodies with the same acceleration must have the same net force. no. the constraint can make their accelerations equal while newton ii gives different net forces m_a a and m_b a when the masses differ.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-nlm-fbd-body-ownership core1a a free-body diagram belongs to one chosen body a free-body diagram contains forces acting on one chosen body only; the equal-and-opposite partner of an interaction acts on the other body and belongs on that other body's diagram. equal and opposite partner forces cancel each other on one body's free-body diagram. choose one body first. put only forces acting on that body on its diagram; draw the partner force only when the other body is chosen. after resolving weight on an incline, mg, mg sin(theta) and mg cos(theta) are three separate forces on the block. no. weight remains one physical force. its parallel/perpendicular components are the coordinate representation used in the chosen equations; do not add the original mg again to those component sums.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-nlm-forces-sum-zero core1a nonzero forces can cancel several nonzero forces can act on one body while their directed sum is zero; the motion responds to the net result rather than to the mere presence of forces. if the net force is zero, no forces are acting. list every interaction force on the body, then combine their directions; cancellation belongs to the net result, not to the individual forces.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-nlm-frame-choice core1a an accelerating observer needs a declared pseudo-force convention a force-based account depends on the observer: a non-accelerating observer uses the physical interaction forces, while an accelerating observer must add the corresponding pseudo-force convention to describe the same observed motion consistently. the same ordinary-force diagram can be used unchanged in any accelerating observer's frame. state the observer first. use physical interactions alone for a non-accelerating observer; for an accelerating observer include the corresponding pseudo-force consistently.

artifacts.subject: Physics
artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-nlm-friction-quant core1a quantitative static and kinetic friction conditions static friction is a responsive contact force: solve for the friction required to prevent relative slip and compare it with the limiting value mu_s n. equality is a threshold condition, while the kinetic model is used only after sliding is established. friction always equals mu n. no. first solve the force required for no slip. static friction matches that requirement up to its limit; equality occurs only at impending slip. the normal force is always mg. determine n from the perpendicular free-body equation. n = mg is only a special case. if both mu_s and mu_k are given, the coefficients themselves tell you which friction model to use. no. determine the contact state first: test whether the no-slip friction demand fits within mu_s n. use the kinetic model only after sliding is established.

artifacts.subject: Physics

artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-wep-energy-derivations core1b derive kinetic and raised-body potential energy from the work ledger the grade 9 energy expressions follow from previously owned mechanics: constant-force work plus newton/kinematics yields the change in kinetic energy, while a controlled lift against near-earth weight yields the increase m g h in gravitational potential energy. k = 0.5 m v^2 and m g h are definitions that cannot be connected to earlier mechanics. for k, combine w_net = f_net s, f_net = m a and v^2-u^2 = 2as. for raised-body u_g, use a slow lift where f_applied = m g and w_applied = f_applied h.

artifacts.search_text: mic-phy-wep-net-work-sign core1b net work sign tracks kinetic-energy change the combined work of all acting forces determines the direction of kinetic-energy change: positive net work increases it, zero net work leaves it unchanged, and negative net work decreases it. only a positive force magnitude can increase kinetic energy; negative work cannot be represented physically. combine the work of all acting forces to obtain net work, then match its sign to whether kinetic energy increases, stays unchanged, or decreases.

artifacts.search_text: q-phy-kin-2d-2a-constant-accel-02 core2a a particle starts with velocity (3 i + 4 j) m/s and has constant acceleration (2 i - 1 j) m/s^2 for 3 s. find its velocity and displacement after 3 s. fam-phy-kin-2d-practice r-kin-2d-ca-model connect apply v=u+at and displacement=ut+(1/2)at^2 separately to x and y while preserving signs and the common time. the given acceleration vector is constant, so each cartesian acceleration component is constant over the same interval and the 1d relations apply component-wise.

artifacts.search_text: q-phy-kin-2d-2a-horizontal-launch-04 core2a split one plane-motion event into independent x/y components with one clock perpendicular components may be solved separately because each axis equation contains only that axis's quantities, but they still describe one object at one physical time. a stone is launched horizontally at 15 m/s from a cliff 20 m above level ground. take +y upward and g=10 m/s^2. find the flight time, horizontal range and impact velocity. fam-phy-kin-2d-practice r-kin-launch-event independent x and y motions may use different elapsed times. no. independence separates the axis equations; it does not give the same object two clocks. the x-motion and y-motion are two different objects that can be paired arbitrarily later. no. a plane state is a simultaneous pair. recombine x(t) and y(t) only at the same t in the same frame. decide use the vertical ground-contact condition delta y=-20 m to determine the flight time before calculating horizontal range or impact velocity. ground impact is defined by the vertical displacement, so the y equation identifies the event time; that one time then belongs to every component at impact.

artifacts.search_text: q-phy-kin-2d-2a-projectile-apex-03 core2a an ideal projectile is launched with already-resolved components u_x=12 m/s and u_y=20 m/s. take +y upward and g=10 m/s^2. find the time to the apex, the velocity at the apex, the acceleration at the apex, and the height gained above launch. fam-phy-kin-2d-practice r-kin-2d-apex-event decide identify the apex by v_y=0, not by setting the full velocity or acceleration to zero. at a vertical turning point v_y changes sign, while horizontal motion continues and gravity remains present.

artifacts.search_text: q-phy-kin-2d-2a-same-height-05 core2a an ideal projectile is launched and later lands at the same height with u_x=12 m/s, u_y=16 m/s and g=8 m/s^2. find the total flight time, range and landing velocity. fam-phy-kin-2d-practice r-kin-2d-same-event decide choose the nonzero root of the vertical event equation as the landing time and reject t=0 as the launch event. the equation describes two visits to the launch height; event identity selects the later root because the question asks for landing.

artifacts.search_text: q-phy-kin-2d-2a-shared-clock-01 core2a a tracker reports x(t)=4t metres and y(t)=10-2t^2 metres for one particle in one fixed frame. find the particle's position at t=2 s, and explain why x(2 s) may not be paired with y(3 s) to describe one position. fam-phy-kin-2d-practice r-kin-2d-clock-pair connect pair the two simultaneous values as the position (8,2) m and reject x(2) paired with y(3) as a single physical state. coordinates form one state only when they refer to the same object, frame and instant; changing one timestamp changes the event.

artifacts.search_text: q-phy-nlm-incline-2a-static-02 core2a quantitative static and kinetic friction conditions static friction is a responsive contact force: solve for the friction required to prevent relative slip and compare it with the limiting value mu_s n. equality is a threshold condition, while the kinetic model is used only after sliding is established. a block rests on a rough fixed plane inclined at angle theta. the coefficient of static friction is mu_s. determine the friction required for rest and derive the condition under which the static state is possible. fam-phy-nlm-incline-modelling r-nlm-incline-static-feasibility friction always equals mu n. no. first solve the force required for no slip. static friction matches that requirement up to its limit; equality occurs only at impending slip. the normal force is always mg. determine n from the perpendicular free-body equation. n = mg is only a special case. if both mu_s and mu_k are given, the coefficients themselves tell you which friction model to use. no. determine the contact state first: test whether the no-slip friction demand fits within mu_s n. use the kinetic model only after sliding is established. decide compare the required friction magnitude with the static limit and accept the rest model only if |f_required| <= mu_s n. the canonical static-friction relation permits the required no-slip value only while its magnitude stays within mu_s n.

artifacts.search_text: q-phy-kin-2d-2b-representation-01 core2b a particle is described verbally: at t=0 it is at the origin, moving east at 6 m/s and north at 2 m/s; during the next interval its acceleration is 3 m/s^2 south and zero east-west. without being given component equations, choose a coordinate convention and write the signed component state that should be used for later calculation. fam-phy-kin-2d-practice r-kin-2d-brep-frame decide choose and declare one perpendicular positive-axis convention before converting the directional facts into signed components. component signs have meaning only relative to an explicitly chosen frame, and this task deliberately withholds that representation decision.

artifacts.search_text: q-phy-kin-2d-2b-same-height-velocity-05 core2b an ideal projectile passes the same height once on the way up and once on the way down. without calculating the times, compare v_x, v_y, speed and acceleration at those two events. fam-phy-kin-2d-practice r-kin-2d-bstate-decide decide choose direct component invariants at equal height as the comparison method instead of solving for the two event times. in ideal flight a_x=0 fixes v_x, while constant vertical acceleration gives equal vertical speed magnitude at the same height; ascent and descent determine opposite signs.
